title: Philippine traffic sign detection
methods: YOLO-format bounding boxes mapped to five classes; training balanced to 605 images (121 per class).
YOLOv8n fine-tuned for 80 epochs at 640-pixel input size; fixed-threshold evaluation uses confidence 0.70 and NMS IoU 0.70.
Rule-based displayed suggestions accompany detected signs; no physical robot control.
summary: YOLOv8n detection of five Philippine traffic-sign classes, with validation and external-dataset evaluation.
results: Notebook saved validation: 386 images, precision/recall/F1 0.997409 at confidence 0.70; mAP50 0.995; mAP50-95 0.854614.
Notebook saved external: 265 images, precision 0.865591, recall 0.607547, F1 0.713969; mAP50 0.731875; mAP50-95 0.52286.
limitations: Additional modules, evaluation files and trained checkpoint referenced by the notebook are not included; the standalone webcam application is unavailable from the published files alone.
External-test recall is 0.6075, substantially below validation recall; results cover only five classes.
attribution: Robopuff Girls: Agnote, Rovilyn Doroin, Ivy; Moico, Mary Joyce; Olivares, Tischia Ann (repository owner); Quite, Rona Mae; Tercero, Michelle. Names follow the published README.

title: Robopuff: Line Follower Robot
subject: Robotics
methods: Five active-low digital inputs on A0–A4 are sampled every 50 ms using millis().
Center detection, or both near-side sensors, selects forward motion; left/right detection selects a pivot turn.
Motor direction pins 8–11 and PWM pins 3/5 control two drive sides; serial output reports sensor state and direction.
summary: A collaborative Arduino robot controller using five digital line-sensor inputs and differential motor steering.
results: Source implements forward motion at PWM 140 and asymmetric turning at PWM 80/100. These are control settings, not measured speed.
An actual prototype photograph and a local demonstration video are available. No lap time, tracking accuracy or success-rate measurement is documented.
limitations: No explicit stop or recovery branch when all sensors lose the line; the previous motor command persists.
The supplied photograph shows an ultrasonic/servo-equipped prototype; the five line-sensor array and exact wiring are not visible, so the photo does not verify the firmware hardware configuration.
Individual responsibilities are not documented in the supplied source. Video participant permissions are unconfirmed.

title: Fuzzy Logic Obstacle Avoidance Robot
subject: Robotics
methods: Single-sensor version scans left/right with a servo and computes near/far memberships over the 20–50 cm transition. A dominant-rule function returns a direction.
Three-sensor version uses NewPing for left/front/right ranges, Fuzzy.h memberships and four rules; defuzzification selects forward, turn, reverse or stop branches.
Three-sensor code maps no-echo readings to 200 cm and updates after a 300 ms delay. Two PWM motor channels drive the chassis.
summary: Two Arduino implementations of reactive obstacle avoidance: a servo-scanned single ultrasonic sensor and a three-sensor fuzzy controller.
results: Two separate source implementations define distance-based motor control. The provided photograph shows three forward-facing ultrasonic modules.
A local group video exists; no quantified collision rate, route-completion rate or navigation-time benchmark is documented.
limitations: In the single-sensor caller, every fuzzy decision other than RIGHT becomes a left turn, including FORWARD and REVERSE.
PWM use on A3/A4 in the single-sensor sketch needs checking against the actual board; no-echo-as-far behavior needs hardware testing.
Individual roles are not stated in the available source files. Video sharing rights and participant permissions are unconfirmed.
attribution: Collaborative academic project by Tischia Ann Olivares, Michelle Tercero and Rona Mae Quite, confirmed by the author. Individual task assignments are not documented.
concerns: Group 11 ownership and participant consent require review.
evidence: Historical saved results and source inspection; experiments and hardware were not rerun.

title: Fashion-MNIST CNN Optimizer Comparison
subject: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
methods: Normalize 28×28 grayscale inputs and add a channel dimension.
Three Conv2D layers (64/128/256 filters, 5×5, same padding) alternate with max pooling; Flatten, Dense(256) and a ten-class softmax complete the model.
Each optimizer uses learning rate 0.001, 10 epochs, batch size 32 and validation_split=0.33; SGD uses momentum 0.9.
summary: A comparison of SGD with momentum, Adam and RMSProp on a shared CNN architecture for ten-class Fashion-MNIST classification.
results: Historical model.evaluate test accuracy: SGD 0.8850; Adam 0.9047; RMSProp 0.9013.
Training/validation curves and sampled prediction comparisons are saved in the original notebook.
limitations: Single runs do not establish multi-seed uncertainty or optimizer superiority across settings.

title: Climate-Based Crop Yield Estimation Using Artificial Neural Networks
subject: Machine Learning
methods: The report describes a synthetic 10,000-row Climate Change Impact on Agriculture dataset; source drops missing rows and selects four climate features.
Dense 128 → 64 → 32 ReLU layers with dropout 0.4/0.3 and a linear scalar output; Adam, MSE loss, batch size 32 and up to 100 epochs.
An 80/20 split reserves test data; the remaining training portion is split again for validation (64/16/20 overall). Early stopping uses validation loss with patience 10.
The notebook compares the ANN with linear regression and random forest, and includes correlation plots and prediction examples.
features: Explore relationships between temperature, precipitation, CO₂ emissions and extreme-weather events
Train an ANN to estimate crop yield in metric tons per hectare
Compare historical ANN performance with linear regression and random forest
summary: A feedforward neural-network regression study estimating crop yield from four climate-related variables on synthetic agricultural data.
results: Report and saved notebook — ANN test MAE 0.7285 MT/ha, RMSE 0.8594 MT/ha and R² 0.3003.
Saved notebook comparison — random forest: MAE 0.746094, RMSE 0.888529, R² 0.252008; linear regression: MAE 0.814171, RMSE 0.992408, R² 0.066889.
The ANN explains approximately 30% of the target variance in this saved synthetic-data test; no field deployment or real-farm validation is documented.
limitations: The dataset is synthetic; results do not establish generalization to real farms or future climate conditions.
StandardScaler is fit before train/test splitting in the source, exposing preprocessing to test-distribution information. The historical metrics are retained with this limitation.
Only one saved split is shown; limited explained variance and no cross-validation constrain conclusions.
Agricultural planning applications discussed in the report are prospective uses, not implemented operational decision-support features.
attribution: Tischia Ann R. Olivares — Individual Academic Project; sole author identified in the final Machine Learning report.
concerns: Synthetic data and preprocessing leakage limit interpretation.
evidence: Historical report and notebook metrics agree; no model training or experiments rerun.
